stem: The review asks students to compare 9/11's aftermath with earlier wartime expansions of federal power. Which comparison is most valid?

explanation: The pattern is one of American history's most tested: war and fear expand the state's reach — jailing dissenters in 1917–18, interning Japanese Americans in 1942, hunting alleged communists in the 1950s — and each expansion is later judged, narrowed, or apologized for. option_explanations.C: Correct. It names three genuine precedents and the shared structure: crisis, expansion, and eventual reckoning.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The act expanded surveillance and detention powers; it did not shrink the federal government.

stem: When Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in the Soviet Union, he pursued glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). What problems was he trying to fix?

(B) The stagnation of the Soviet command economy and the rigidity of one-party rule.
(C) A dangerous shortage of Soviet nuclear weapons relative to the American arsenal.
(D) An excess of political freedom enjoyed by ordinary Soviet citizens.
explanation: By the 1980s the Soviet economy had barely grown for a decade: central planning could not innovate, farms and factories were inefficient, and the party bureaucracy smothered initiative. Gorbachev's reforms were an insider's attempt to save the system by loosening it — an attempt that instead helped bring it down.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Soviets were not winning victories; their costly stalemate in Afghanistan was one symptom of the overreach Gorbachev inherited.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Economic stagnation and political rigidity were exactly the twin crises glasnost and perestroika were designed to address.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The USSR possessed a vast nuclear arsenal; weapons quantity was not the problem — economic decay was.

stem: The INF Treaty of 1987, signed by Reagan and Gorbachev, was historic for which reason?

(C) It admitted the Soviet Union as a full member of NATO.
(D) It was signed before Reagan had ever criticized the Soviet Union publicly.
explanation: Earlier arms agreements had capped how many weapons each side could hold; the INF Treaty went further, destroying every U.S. and Soviet missile with a range of 500 to 5,500 kilometers. It showed that Reagan's confrontation and his diplomacy were two phases of one strategy: pressure first, then a deal with a reforming Soviet leader.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The treaty's distinction was elimination rather than limitation — an entire category of weapons destroyed and verified by on-site inspection.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Both superpowers kept thousands of strategic nuclear weapons; only intermediate-range missiles were eliminated.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Soviet Union never joined NATO; the alliance remained a Western institution throughout the Cold War.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Reagan signed the treaty in 1987, four years after the 1983 'evil empire' speech — the criticism came first, the diplomacy second.

stem: The Iran-Contra affair, exposed in 1986, involved the secret, illegal sale of arms to Iran to fund Contra rebels in Nicaragua. What did the affair most clearly reveal about the Reagan administration?
options: (A) That the administration had no interest in Central America or its conflicts.
(B) That officials pursued anti-communist goals outside the law, deceiving Congress and the public.
(C) That Congress had authorized every part of the operation in advance.
(D) That the affair actually strengthened the administration's reputation for strict and careful legal compliance.
explanation: Congress had cut off aid to the Contras; administration officials evaded that restriction by secretly selling arms to Iran — itself under an arms embargo — and diverting the profits. The scandal showed the tension between the administration's anti-communist zeal and constitutional limits, damaging Reagan's standing even though he survived it politically.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The affair proves the opposite: the administration cared enough about Nicaragua to break the law over it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It names what the investigations established: an off-the-books foreign policy run around Congress's explicit restrictions.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Evading Congress was the scandal's core; the operation was concealed precisely because Congress had forbidden Contra aid.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The affair produced criminal convictions of administration officials and a lasting stain on the administration's legal reputation.

stem: In 1989, communist governments fell across Eastern Europe in rapid succession. What Soviet decision made those revolutions possible?
options: (A) The Soviet Union sent tanks into every Eastern European capital to defend the regimes, but the tanks broke down en route.
(B) Gorbachev ordered the construction of a new Berlin Wall to contain the unrest.
(C) The Soviet Union had already dissolved before 1989, so no decision was needed.
(D) Gorbachev refused to use Soviet force against the uprisings, abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine of past invasions.
explanation: Eastern European regimes had survived for decades because Moscow would intervene — as in Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968). When Gorbachev made clear in 1989 that Soviet tanks would not come, the regimes' enforcers lost their nerve and crowds filled the streets. The empire's outer ring fell because its center chose not to defend it.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. No such invasions occurred in 1989; the absence of Soviet force, not its failure, is what mattered.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Gorbachev did not build walls; the existing one was torn down by the crowds his non-intervention enabled.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, two years after the Eastern European revolutions.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It identifies the decisive change: the repudiation of the Brezhnev Doctrine removed the threat that had kept the satellite regimes in power.

stem: After 1991, some commentators declared the 'end of history' — the permanent triumph of liberal democracy over all rivals. Which later development best challenges that claim?
options: (A) Great-power rivalry returned, authoritarian states endured, and Western democracies polarized deeply after 2010.
(B) The complete disappearance of all authoritarian governments by the year 2000.
(C) The unanimous global adoption of American-style democracy, with every nation converting during the 1990s without a single exception anywhere.
(D) The end of all international conflict after the Cold War ended.
explanation: The 'end of history' thesis mistook a moment for a destination. The decades after 1991 brought a more assertive Russia and China, authoritarian regimes that survived and adapted, and — as the review stresses — institutional distrust and polarization inside the United States itself, including the January 6 attack on the Capitol. Liberal democracy's victory was neither complete nor permanent.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It cites the actual record the review describes — the failure to build a new consensus, polarization, institutional distrust — as evidence against permanent triumph.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Authoritarian governments persisted and in some cases strengthened after 1991; they did not disappear.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. No such unanimous adoption occurred; many states adopted democratic forms briefly or not at all.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The post–Cold War era saw the Gulf War, the Balkans, Afghanistan, Iraq, and many other conflicts.

stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending at $299 billion in 1990, higher than its 1988 level of $290 billion. What does this suggest about the 'peace dividend' many Americans expected after the Cold War?

options: (A) The peace dividend arrived immediately and completely, with American military spending falling all the way to zero in 1990, ending the defense budget entirely.
(B) The dividend disappointed: spending held near Cold War peaks as the USSR collapsed, and new interventions added fresh demands.
(C) Military spending had never risen in the first place, so no dividend was possible.
(D) The chart proves the Cold War never actually ended.
explanation: The chart shows the buildup's momentum carrying past the Cold War's end: 1990 spending was the highest plotted. Some cuts did come in the 1990s, but the Gulf War, the Balkans, and later Afghanistan and Iraq kept America globally entangled — the 'victory lap' never produced the deep demobilization many had imagined.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The chart shows $299 billion in 1990, the highest value plotted — not zero and not falling.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It reads the chart accurately (spending still at peak as the USSR collapsed) and connects it to the interventions that absorbed the would-be savings.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The chart documents a dramatic rise from $134 to $299 billion; the buildup plainly happened.

stem: Which internal development most directly caused the Soviet Union itself — not just its Eastern European satellites — to dissolve in December 1991?
options: (A) Independence movements in the Baltics, Ukraine, and beyond hollowed out the union from within.
(B) The United States invaded the Soviet Union in 1991 and dissolved it by force.
(C) Gorbachev abolished the entire Soviet military, leaving the vast country completely defenseless against invasion.
(D) The Soviet economy was booming, so the republics saw no reason to remain.
explanation: The USSR was a multi-ethnic empire, and glasnost uncorked nationalisms the party had suppressed for decades. As Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Ukraine, and others declared sovereignty, Moscow's authority evaporated republic by republic; by December 1991 there was no union left for Gorbachev to preside over, whatever Washington did or didn't do.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It identifies the proximate internal mechanism: secessionist nationalism dissolving the federation from inside, the distinct final step after Eastern Europe's breakaway.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The United States never invaded the Soviet Union; the dissolution was an internal political collapse.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Gorbachev kept the armed forces intact; they simply would not — and could not — hold the union together.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The economy was stagnating badly; economic failure fueled the republics' exit rather than preventing it.

stem: With the Soviet Union gone, the review says America 'stood alone as the unchallenged superpower.' What did this unipolar moment mean for American foreign policy in the 1990s?
options: (A) The United States withdrew from the world and adopted strict isolationism.
(B) American foreign policy became identical to Soviet foreign policy in every respect, goal, and method.
(C) The United Nations was abolished as unnecessary in the new era.
(D) The U.S. faced fewer great-power constraints after 1991 and undertook interventions to uphold a liberal order.
explanation: Unipolarity removed the Soviet veto — literal, at the UN, and strategic, in every crisis. Washington used that freedom to lead coalitions against Iraq and later in the Balkans, presenting American power as the enforcer of a rules-based order. The 'new world order' was unipolarity's doctrine: one superpower managing the peace.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The 1990s were an active interventionist decade, the opposite of isolationism.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. American policy pursued liberal-order goals alien to Soviet practice; the two were not interchangeable.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The UN remained central — the Gulf War was fought under its authorization — and was not abolished.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It captures what unipolarity enabled: American-led collective action without a rival bloc to block or balance it.

stem: The Cold War policy of containment committed the United States to resisting communist expansion. Which post–Cold War American action shows the strongest continuity with that tradition?
options: (A) The adoption of strict isolationism, the closing of every overseas base, and the withdrawal of all American forces to within national borders.
(B) The abolition of the armed forces after 1991.
(C) A refusal to participate in any international coalition or alliance.
(D) Leading coalitions against aggression (Iraq in Kuwait) and atrocities (the Balkans), extending intervention to new causes.
explanation: Containment built the machinery and the mindset: America as the organizer of coalitions against aggression. After 1991 the enemy changed but the habit persisted — Washington still assembled alliances and projected force, now in the name of international order rather than anti-communism.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The United States did not adopt isolationism; the 1990s were an interventionist decade with bases retained worldwide.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The armed forces were reduced but remained the world's largest and most capable military.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Gulf War coalition is the textbook counterexample: dozens of nations acting together under American leadership.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It identifies the continuity: the institutional habit of American-led collective action, repurposed from containing communism to policing the post–Cold War order.

options: (A) The internal-decay interpretation: economic failure and nationalist secession as the primary drivers of collapse.

(D) The interpretation that the Soviet economy was outperforming the American economy in 1991.

That is the internal-decay school in miniature — useful to a historian mapping the debate's positions, though not proof the school is right.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The passage's two named causes — economic failure and nationalist secession — are exactly the internal-decay interpretation's pillars.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The passage's first sentence explicitly rejects invasion as the cause.

options: (A) The United States produced no oil at all, so the price change did not affect its economy.
(B) America's flexible market economy absorbed the shock; the Soviet command economy depended on oil exports and could not adapt.
(C) The Soviet Union's economy was far more diversified and flexible than America's, so it absorbed the price shock easily.
(D) Oil prices did not actually change in the 1980s, according to the chart.

The Soviet system could not reallocate — its rigid planning and dependence on a single export for foreign earnings turned the same price swing into a fiscal catastrophe.

stem: The chart shows crude oil prices falling by roughly a third in the mid-1980s. How did this price collapse compound the cost of the Soviet war in Afghanistan (1979–1989)?

options: (A) The price collapse made the war cheaper for Moscow, since armies run on oil.
(B) Afghanistan paid the Soviet Union in regular oil shipments, making the long war profitable for Moscow overall.
(C) Falling oil revenues left Moscow less able to afford the stalemated war, deepening the 'bleeding wound.'
(D) The war ended in 1980, before prices fell, so the two were unrelated.
explanation: Gorbachev himself called Afghanistan a 'bleeding wound.' The war consumed money, men, and morale for a decade; when the oil-price collapse simultaneously drained the revenue that funded the Soviet state, the combination of a costly stalemate abroad and a fiscal crisis at home made withdrawal the only rational choice — completed in 1989.

stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending nearly doubling between 1980 and 1985. A student claims that the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) alone ended the Cold War. Which rebuttal is strongest?

options: (A) SDI was fully deployed in 1985, and its orbital lasers destroyed the entire Soviet nuclear arsenal within months.
(B) Soviet leaders never heard of SDI, so it could not have affected their decisions.
(C) SDI single-handedly caused the Berlin Wall to fall in 1989.
(D) SDI was never built and ended nothing by itself; the chart's broad buildup was only one cause among many.

stem: German reunification in 1990 mattered beyond Germany itself for which reason?
options: (A) It erased the Cold War's central dividing line in Europe, confirming that the postwar order was over.
(B) It restored the German monarchy that had ruled before 1918.
(C) It caused the United States to withdraw from NATO immediately after reunification, ending the American commitment to Europe.
(D) It had no significance outside Germany's own borders.
explanation: Divided Germany was the Cold War's physical embodiment: the line where the two blocs faced each other. Reunification — achieved peacefully and inside NATO — meant the division of Europe itself was ending, not just one country's internal arrangement.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It states the wider significance: reunification was the continent's reunification in miniature, the moment the Iron Curtain's central front dissolved.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Reunification created no monarchy; the united Germany remained the democratic Federal Republic.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The United States stayed in NATO, and reunified Germany stayed in it too — a key condition Moscow reluctantly accepted.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Few events of 1990 mattered more internationally; it redrew Europe's map and confirmed the Cold War's end.

stem: NATO survived the Cold War while the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact dissolved. Which explanation best accounts for NATO's persistence?

(B) NATO was a voluntary alliance and its members kept it; the Warsaw Pact was imposed by Moscow and died with Soviet power.
(C) The Soviet Union joined NATO in 1992, keeping the alliance alive.
(D) NATO persisted because its members were legally forbidden from ever leaving the alliance under the treaty's terms.
explanation: Alliances held together by consent outlast those held together by coercion. NATO members — democracies that had joined voluntarily — found continued value in the alliance for the Balkans and beyond; the Warsaw Pact, an instrument of Soviet domination, disintegrated the moment Moscow stopped enforcing it.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. NATO was not abolished; it remains active decades after the Cold War's end.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It identifies the structural difference: voluntary alliance versus imposed bloc, which explains their different fates.

stem: President George H. W. Bush's management of the Cold War's end is often praised by historians for which quality?
options: (A) Rushing to humiliate the Soviet leadership as thoroughly as possible.
(B) Refusing all dealings with Gorbachev throughout the crisis, boycotting every summit, call, and negotiation entirely.
(C) Cautious stewardship: backing reunification in NATO without humiliating Moscow, lest hardliners gain strength.
(D) Ordering an American invasion of Eastern Europe in 1990.
explanation: Bush understood that a cornered nuclear superpower was dangerous. He pressed American advantages — reunified Germany in NATO — but gave Gorbachev face-saving cooperation, economic aid discussions, and partnership rhetoric, denying Soviet hardliners the provocation that could have justified a crackdown or coup attempt.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Humiliation was what Bush deliberately avoided; triumphalism, he feared, would strengthen the Kremlin's hardliners.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Bush dealt with Gorbachev extensively, meeting him at summits including Malta in 1989.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It describes the actual stewardship: firm on Western goals, careful about Soviet dignity — the prudence historians credit for the Cold War's peaceful end.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No such invasion occurred or was contemplated; American policy worked through diplomacy, not force, in Eastern Europe.

stem: Unlike the two World Wars, the Cold War ended without a formal peace treaty or settlement conference. What consequence followed from that difference?

(B) No postwar rules were agreed, so NATO's role and Russia's place stayed unsettled — the 'failure to build a new consensus.'
(C) The United States and Russia became close allies immediately after 1991, with no disagreements between them on any issue whatsoever.
(D) All nuclear weapons were automatically abolished when the Soviet Union dissolved.

option_explanations.B: Correct. It connects the missing settlement to the review's central theme: the end of the old consensus without a new one to replace it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. U.S.-Russian relations were cooperative briefly, then deteriorated sharply; no close alliance resulted.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Russia inherited the Soviet nuclear arsenal; disarmament required separate treaties and remained incomplete.

(B) Latino voters acted as a single bloc with no internal political differences of any kind, voting identically.
(C) Immigration disappeared as an issue in American politics after 2000.
(D) Both parties increasingly competed for Latino voters, making immigration a central electoral battleground nationwide.
explanation: Demographic change reshaped the electorate, and parties responded strategically. As the Latino vote grew in states such as California, Texas, and Florida, both Democrats and Republicans courted it — which is why immigration enforcement, legalization, and border policy became fiercely contested campaign issues rather than settled ones.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Parties courted Latino voters actively; ignoring a fast-growing electorate would have been political malpractice.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Latino voters differ by national origin, generation, and region — Cuban Americans, Mexican Americans, and Puerto Ricans have distinct political profiles.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Immigration became more contested, not less, exactly as the review says demographic change 'reshaped politics, especially around immigration.'
option_explanations.D: Correct. It describes the actual dynamic: demographic growth made the group electorally pivotal, and competition over its votes pushed immigration to the center of campaigns.

stem: The review calls Ronald Reagan's 1980 election 'a repudiation.' What was being repudiated?
options: (A) The entire conservative movement, which the voters decisively rejected in favor of a renewed liberalism.
(B) The New Deal/Great Society premise: Washington should actively manage the economy and expand social programs.
(C) The federal government itself, which Reagan then abolished.
(D) American democracy, which voters abandoned in 1980.
explanation: Reagan's victory was ideological, not merely personal. After decades in which liberalism's answer — activist federal government as the engine of security and justice — dominated, voters in 1980 endorsed the opposite answer: government as the problem. The review frames the whole era as this reversal and its long aftermath.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Voters embraced the conservative movement in 1980; they did not reject it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It names what 'repudiation' means here: the rejection of the liberal premise about government's purpose, which the review asks students to contrast with Reagan's conservatism point by point.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Reagan did not abolish the federal government; he redirected and partly shrank it while expanding the military.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The election was an exercise of democracy, not its abandonment.

stem: The review says 'Reaganomics rested on supply-side theory.' What did the theory claim?
options: (A) That government spending is the one and only possible source of economic growth in any economy.
(B) That raising tax rates always increases government revenue.
(C) That lower taxes would unleash enough private-sector growth to fully pay for the cuts themselves.
(D) That the economy works best when money is abolished entirely.
explanation: Supply-side economics inverted the Keynesian logic: instead of stimulating demand through spending, it would stimulate supply — investment, work, enterprise — by letting people keep more of what they earned. The crucial, testable promise was that the resulting growth would generate enough new tax revenue to offset the lower rates.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. That is the Keynesian/demand-side claim; supply-side theory argued the opposite — that private activity, freed from taxes, drives growth.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Supply-siders argued that lower rates could raise revenue through growth; they did not claim that higher rates always raise revenue.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It states the theory's distinctive, falsifiable core: growth paying for the cuts — the promise against which the 1980s deficits are measured.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. This is nonsensical; no economic school advocated abolishing money.

stem: The chart shows the federal deficit at $221 billion in 1986, five years after the 1981 tax cuts. What does this figure show about supply-side theory's central prediction?

(B) The chart is completely irrelevant to evaluating the economic theory and proves absolutely nothing either way.
(C) The deficit fell after the cuts, proving they paid for themselves.
(D) The prediction failed: far from paying for themselves, the cuts were followed by tripled deficits.
explanation: The theory's promise was self-financing growth. The chart's verdict: $74 billion in 1980, $221 billion in 1986 — the deficit roughly tripled. Growth did return, but revenues never caught up with the combination of lower rates and higher defense spending, which is why the review pairs the two outcomes in one sentence.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The chart shows a $221 billion deficit in 1986, not a vanished one.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The deficit is the direct test of whether the cuts paid for themselves; it is the most relevant evidence.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The deficit rose from $74 billion to $221 billion; it did not fall.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It applies the chart's numbers to the theory's promise and reports the result honestly: growth without self-financing.

explanation: The chart's 20.1 percent marks labor's high-water line; what followed was a generation of decline. PATCO was the turning point the review identifies: by crushing a strike of skilled federal workers, Reagan demonstrated that aggressive anti-union tactics would face no federal opposition — and private employers took the lesson into their own labor battles through the 1980s.

stem: 'Government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.' — Ronald Reagan, First Inaugural Address, 1981 (short famous phrase quoted). What did this line signal about Reagan's view of federal power?

stimulus.text: Government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem. — Ronald Reagan, First Inaugural Address, 1981 (short famous phrase quoted).

options: (A) That he planned a dramatic expansion of federal programs.
(B) A reversal: liberals cast Washington as the solver of problems; Reagan cast it as the obstacle.
(C) That he intended to abolish the presidency itself.
(D) That he fully and completely agreed with the liberal view of government's proper role in the economy.
explanation: The line was a philosophical declaration, not a policy detail. For half a century, liberalism's premise had been that federal action fixes what markets and states cannot; Reagan's sentence inverted the premise entirely — the government's attempted solutions were themselves the disease. Everything in the Reagan program, from tax cuts to deregulation, flowed from that inversion.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The line announced retrenchment, not expansion; Reagan sought to shrink domestic government, not grow it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It identifies the sentence as the ideological key to the era: the premise-flip the review asks students to contrast with the liberalism it displaced.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Reagan used the presidency energetically, especially for the military buildup; he did not seek to abolish the office.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The line directly contradicted the liberal view; agreement would have made the sentence meaningless.

stem: The review asks students to contrast Reagan's conservatism with the liberalism it displaced. Which of the following states the contrast accurately?
options: (A) Both sides agreed completely about the proper role of the federal government.
(B) Liberals wanted a much smaller federal government while conservatives wanted a much larger and more powerful one.
(C) Liberals: federal power delivers security and justice. Conservatives: it threatens freedom and growth.
(D) Neither side held any coherent view of what the federal government should do.
explanation: This is the point-by-point contrast the review demands. Liberalism's answer to 'what is government for' — regulate the economy, insure against hardship, expand rights — became, in the conservative telling, the cause of stagnation and lost freedom. The two visions were mirror opposites on the same question.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The era was defined by fundamental disagreement about government's role; agreement is the opposite of the historical record.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the two sides: liberals defended the large federal role, conservatives attacked it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It states the core philosophical inversion cleanly: same question (what is government for), opposite answers.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Both sides held elaborate, coherent — and opposed — philosophies of government.

stem: Deregulation 'accelerated under Reagan across airlines, banking, energy, and communications.' Supporters of deregulation argued that it would do which of the following?
options: (A) Raise consumer prices deliberately in order to protect established companies from competition.
(B) Transfer ownership of the affected industries to the federal government.
(C) Guarantee every worker a lifetime job regardless of business conditions.
(D) Lower prices and more competition by removing rate-setting and entry barriers.
explanation: The deregulatory case was that regulators had become captives of the industries they oversaw, protecting incumbents and inflating prices. Removing rate-setting and entry barriers — as with the breakup-era phone market and discount airlines — would let competition discipline prices instead.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Supporters promised lower prices through competition; protecting incumbents by raising prices was the system they attacked.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Government ownership (nationalization) is the reverse of deregulation, which reduced the state's role.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Deregulation exposed firms to market competition, which tended to weaken job security rather than guarantee it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It states the pro-deregulation argument as its advocates made it: competition replacing regulation as the guardian of the consumer.

stem: The review's verdict on Reaganomics — 'Growth did return, but so did huge deficits and stark inequality' — supports which overall evaluation?
options: (A) A mixed verdict: renewed growth but a failed fiscal promise and wider inequality.
(B) An unqualified triumph with absolutely no significant downsides of any kind whatsoever.
(C) An unqualified failure that produced no economic growth at all.
(D) Proof that economic policy no longer affects the economy.
explanation: The review's single sentence is deliberately two-sided, and honest evaluation must hold both sides: the 1980s expansion was real, and so were the tripled deficits and the stretched income distribution. Reaganomics delivered on growth while failing on its own supply-side promise and on equity — a mixed record that partisans on both sides tend to flatten.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It refuses the partisan simplifications and matches the review's balanced sentence: growth yes, self-financing no, inequality up.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The review explicitly lists huge deficits and stark inequality as outcomes; ignoring them replaces evaluation with cheerleading.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The review states that growth did return; denying it contradicts the record.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The sentence's whole point is that policy choices had large, measurable consequences.

(D) The chart shows budget surpluses throughout the 1980s.
explanation: The chart's unbroken run of positive values — deficits every year, rising to $290 billion by 1992 — is the fiscal signature of the era's policy mix: the 1981 tax cuts reduced revenue while the military buildup raised spending, and no amount of domestic cutting closed the resulting gap.

option_explanations.B: Correct. It names the policy combination behind the chart's sustained deficits, matching the review's account of tax cuts plus military spending.

stem: The chart shows the deficit at $221 billion in 1986 despite Reagan's domestic spending cuts. Why didn't those cuts prevent the deficits?

chart_spec.title: Federal Budget Deficit (+) / Surplus (−), 1980–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; Reagan-era deficits per u9.md §The story ('Growth did return, but so did huge deficits').

options: (A) Reagan never cut any spending whatsoever.
(B) The domestic spending cuts were so enormous that they alone single-handedly caused the entire deficit.
(C) Congress doubled all federal spending in response to the cuts.
(D) Domestic cuts, soaring defense, falling revenues: the savings could not cover the combined gap.
explanation: Arithmetic defeated the program: domestic discretionary spending was never large enough for its cuts to offset a historic tax cut plus a historic military buildup. The chart's $221 billion gap is the remainder after the cuts — proof that shrinking one part of government while growing another does not shrink the deficit.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Reagan did cut many domestic programs substantially; the cuts were real but insufficient.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Cutting spending reduces deficits, all else equal; the deficit came from the tax and defense side of the ledger, not from the cuts.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Congress did not double spending; the deficit's drivers were the tax cuts and the defense buildup.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It does the fiscal arithmetic the chart demands: cuts in one category overwhelmed by growth in the others.

stem: The 1981 tax cut, the Economic Recovery Tax Act, did which of the following?
options: (A) Raised individual income taxes to the highest marginal income-tax rates in all of American history.
(B) Abolished the federal income tax entirely.
(C) Cut individual income-tax rates substantially — the centerpiece of the supply-side program.
(D) Applied only to corporations, leaving individual rates untouched.
explanation: ERTA cut the top individual rate from 70 to 50 percent and reduced rates across the board — the largest tax cut to that point in American history. It was the supply-side theory made law: leave money in private hands and growth would follow.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The act cut rates sharply; it did not raise them.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The income tax survived; rates were reduced, not eliminated.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It describes the act's content and its place as the legislative heart of Reaganomics.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The individual rate cuts were the act's core; corporate provisions were secondary.

stem: The 1980 election offered voters a clear philosophical choice. What were the alternatives?
options: (A) Two candidates who agreed on nearly every issue.
(B) A choice between two different brands of liberalism.
(C) A choice between two different brands of conservatism, with no liberal alternative available to voters.
(D) Carter's active-government liberalism versus Reagan's shrink-at-home and rebuild-the-military conservatism.
explanation: 1980 was the rare election that was genuinely about first principles. Carter, for all his difficulties, defended the liberal premise of energetic federal government; Reagan offered its repudiation — smaller domestic government, lower taxes, and a rearmed America. Voters chose the philosophy, not just the man.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The candidates disagreed fundamentally about government's proper size and role.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Reagan was not a liberal of any brand; he ran against liberalism itself.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Carter was a Democrat defending the liberal order, not a conservative.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It states the philosophical stakes the review's 'repudiation' framing describes.

stem: The chart shows union membership falling from 20.1 percent of workers in 1980 to 13.5 percent in 2000. How does the PATCO episode of 1981 fit into this longer decline?

chart_spec.title: Union Membership as Share of U.S. Workers, 1980–2020
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the decline following the PATCO turning point described in u9.md §Key terms (PATCO strike, 1981, 'a landmark defeat for organized labor').

options: (A) A landmark labor defeat — one cause within a broader decline also driven by restructuring and resistance.
(B) The PATCO firings caused union membership to rise sharply.
(C) The chart shows the PATCO episode had no effect on union membership at all.
(D) Every single American union was dissolved by an act of Congress in 1982, ending organized labor entirely.
explanation: The chart's twenty-year slide needs more than one cause, and historians supply several: the strike's defeat, plant closures, the shift toward service work, and aggressive employer campaigns. PATCO's role was catalytic and symbolic — the review's 'landmark defeat' — within a structural decline, not the sole engine of it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It places PATCO correctly: a genuine turning point inside a multi-causal decline, matching both the chart and the review.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Membership fell, not rose, after 1981 — from 20.1 to 18.0 percent by 1985.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The decline steepened in the 1980s immediately after the firings; dismissing any effect ignores the timing.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Unions continued to exist and represent millions of workers; they shrank but were not abolished.

stem: The review says the Reagan-era recovery brought 'stark inequality' alongside renewed growth. Which development best explains why growth and inequality rose together?
options: (A) Wages for all workers rose equally, so no inequality resulted.
(B) Tax cuts and deregulation favored investors and high earners while ordinary wage growth lagged.
(C) The federal government seized every bit of private wealth in the entire nation and forcibly redistributed it.
(D) Americans stopped working, so only investors earned income.
explanation: The Reagan program's benefits flowed disproportionately upward: lower top tax rates, deregulation's rewards to capital, and the weakening of unions all boosted returns to investors and professionals. Meanwhile, ordinary wage growth was modest — so the economy grew and the income gap widened at the same time, exactly the review's paired outcome.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Wage growth was uneven, with top earners pulling far ahead; equal gains would not produce 'stark inequality.'
option_explanations.B: Correct. It identifies the mechanism linking the era's policies to its distributional result: gains concentrated at the top, stagnation in the middle.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The government did not seize private wealth; the era moved policy in the opposite direction, toward lower taxes.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Employment grew in the 1980s; the issue was the distribution of gains, not a collapse of work.

fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'Growth did return, but so did huge deficits and stark inequality'

stem: Which development best shows that Reagan's conservative shift outlasted his own presidency?
options: (A) The immediate repeal of every Reagan policy in 1989.
(B) A complete return to the 1970s style of liberal governance throughout the entire decade of the 1990s.
(C) A Democratic president declaring 'the era of big government is over' and signing welfare reform in 1996.
(D) The abolition of the Republican Party after Reagan left office.
explanation: Realignments are proven when the other side adapts to them. Clinton's triangulation — balanced budgets, welfare reform, deregulation-friendly policies — showed that the debate's center had moved: even Democrats now had to speak the language of limited government. That is how you know 1980 was a realignment, not a mood.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Reagan's core policies — low top tax rates, deregulation, the military establishment — survived his departure.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The 1990s moved further toward market-friendly, small-government premises, not back to 1970s liberalism.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It cites the review's own evidence of conservative hegemony: a Democratic president internalizing the Reagan-era premises.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Republican Party thrived after Reagan, winning Congress in 1994 and the presidency in 2000.

stem: The chart shows federal deficits in every year from 1980 to 1992. Reagan 'promised to shrink government at home' while 'spending massively on the military abroad.' What did this combination actually produce?

(B) The elimination of the American military.

stem: On taxation, the clearest difference between Reagan's conservatism and the liberalism it displaced was which of the following?
options: (A) Liberals: progressive taxes fund programs and curb inequality. Supply-siders: tax cuts drive growth.
(B) Liberals wanted to abolish every single tax entirely while conservatives wanted to raise them all sharply.
(C) Both sides held identical views on taxation.
(D) Neither side had any position on taxes or fiscal policy.
explanation: For liberals, progressive taxes were how you paid for the New Deal/Great Society commitments and leveled the income distribution. For supply-siders, taxes were the drag on enterprise — cutting them wasn't just fiscal policy but growth policy. The same tax code was, to each side, a completely different instrument.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It states the genuine philosophical divide: taxation as redistribution-and-revenue versus taxation as growth-policy.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses both sides: liberals defended taxation, conservatives attacked it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Taxation was among the sharpest disagreements of the era.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Both sides made taxation central to their economic programs.

stem: The review says 'the New Right reversed the New Deal/Great Society answer to what government is for.' What did that reversal mean in practice?
options: (A) The New Right massively expanded federal social programs far beyond their Great Society levels.
(B) The New Right left the New Deal/Great Society framework completely untouched.
(C) New Deal: Washington guarantees security. New Right: limiting Washington is the goal.
(D) The New Right abolished the presidency.
explanation: The reversal was programmatic, not just rhetorical: each New Deal/Great Society instrument got a conservative mirror image — progressive taxation answered by tax cuts, regulation answered by deregulation, federal programs answered by devolution to states. The review's 'reversed the answer' is literal: the same question, the opposite policy in every domain.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The New Right cut and constrained federal social programs; it did not expand them.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The New Right's entire project was dismantling or limiting that framework.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It translates the philosophical reversal into its concrete policies: tax cuts, deregulation, devolution — the Reagan program's three domestic pillars.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The presidency continued; what changed was the philosophy guiding its use.

stem: Reagan's conservative coalition brought together which of the following groups?
options: (A) Only and exclusively Wall Street bankers, with absolutely no other supporters of any kind whatsoever.
(B) Only active-duty military officers.
(C) Only residents of California.
(D) Business, anti-communists, repudiation voters: united as much by opposition as by favor.

Each group got its priority, which is why the coalition held despite their differences.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Business was one leg of the coalition, but the military buildup and the broader repudiation of liberalism drew far wider support.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Anti-communism attracted many civilians; the coalition was not limited to the military.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Reagan won nationally, carrying 44 states in 1980; his coalition was not a regional one.

stem: For ordinary consumers, deregulation's most visible effects in the 1980s included which of the following?
options: (A) The end of all commercial air travel.
(B) Government ownership of the telephone companies.
(C) Cheaper long-distance calls and airfares as market competition replaced government-set rates.
(D) Higher prices for every single deregulated service across the board, without any exception.
explanation: Deregulation's consumer payoff was concrete and popular: the breakup-era phone market drove long-distance rates down year after year, and airline deregulation brought discount carriers and fare wars. These visible wins helped sell the broader deregulatory program politically.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Air travel expanded enormously after deregulation; it did not end.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The trend was away from government control — the AT&T breakup being the landmark — not toward ownership.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It names the two textbook consumer benefits of 1980s deregulation: cheaper calls and cheaper flights.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Prices fell in the most prominently deregulated consumer industries, which was the policy's selling point.

stem: The chart shows the federal deficit rising from $74 billion in 1980 to $221 billion in 1986. Which criticism of Reaganomics is best supported by the review's own account?

explanation: The fairest criticism uses the theory's own standard: supply-side economics promised self-financing growth, and the chart shows the opposite — $74 billion to $221 billion. stem: Reagan's domestic spending cuts targeted which of the following?
options: (A) Military spending, which was slashed to near zero.
(B) Social Security, which the new administration completely abolished during its very first year in office.
(C) Tax collection, which the administration ended.
(D) Great Society social programs, while defense grew — reversing the 1960s priorities.
explanation: The cuts had a philosophy: programs born of the Great Society — antipoverty spending, urban aid, job training, environmental and consumer regulation budgets — were the targets, while the Pentagon's budget soared. It was the New Right's reversal made fiscal: the 1960s had grown domestic government, the 1980s grew military government.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Military spending grew enormously; it was the one budget category clearly exempt from the knife.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Social Security survived; it was too popular to abolish, though Reagan did trim some benefits.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Tax collection continued; the IRS was not abolished.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It describes the actual pattern: domestic social spending cut, defense spending raised — the fiscal expression of the era's reprioritization.

stem: Historians summarizing Reagan's domestic legacy often cite three developments together: the PATCO defeat, large deficits, and rising inequality. What connects the three?
options: (A) All three were caused entirely by foreign governments.
(B) The three had nothing in common with one another.
(C) All three expressed the rebalancing: labor→employers, revenue→debt, middle→top.
(D) All three were pure accidents of history with no relation to any policy choices whatsoever.
explanation: The three are one story told three ways. PATCO shifted workplace power toward employers; the tax-cut-plus-buildup fiscal mix shifted government's financing from revenue to borrowing; and both shifts moved income upward. Together they describe what the Reagan revolution redistributed — money and, just as importantly, leverage.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. All three were products of domestic American policy choices, not foreign action.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The three share the era's signature: a systematic shift of power and resources upward and rightward.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It synthesizes the three into the era's single domestic narrative: the rebalancing of power from labor, from revenue, and from the middle.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Each followed directly from deliberate policies: the PATCO firings, the 1981 tax cuts, and the deregulatory program.

stem: Franklin Roosevelt held that government must act to secure citizens' welfare; Reagan held that government was the problem. Their core disagreement was over which question?
options: (A) Whether federal power cures economic insecurity or causes it.
(B) Whether the United States should continue to exist.
(C) Whether presidents should be allowed to give speeches to the public at all.
(D) They had no significant disagreement whatsoever.
explanation: Strip away the decades and the policies, and the two presidents answered one question oppositely. Roosevelt's answer built the New Deal state; Reagan's answer launched the project of dismantling it. Every specific fight — over taxes, regulation, welfare — was this philosophical disagreement in policy form.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It reduces the Roosevelt-Reagan contrast to its philosophical core, the same contrast the review asks students to draw point by point.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Neither president questioned the nation's existence; they disagreed about government's role within it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Both were celebrated communicators; oratory was not their disagreement.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Their disagreement defined American politics for half a century.

stem: The review says Reagan broke the 1981 PATCO strike 'to signal that organized labor's power was over.' What made that signal credible to private employers watching the episode?
options: (A) He praised the strikers and granted all their demands.
(B) He ignored the strike entirely and let it continue.
(C) Congress immediately overruled the president and rehired every single controller with full back pay.
(D) Skilled, irreplaceable strikers broken; traffic kept running. Even strong unions could fall.
explanation: Signals work when they're costly. Air-traffic controllers were not easily replaced — yet Reagan replaced them, decertified their union, and banned them from federal service for life. Private employers drew the obvious lesson: if the government could do that to skilled federal workers, they could take a hard line with their own unions — and through the 1980s, they did.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Reagan fired the strikers; he did not meet their demands.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Reagan acted within days, giving the strikers 48 hours to return before firing them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Congress did not overrule the firings; the controllers stayed fired.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It identifies why the example was so powerful: the difficulty of the feat proved the seriousness of the intent.

stem: Some historians call Reagan's 1980 victory a 'revolution' rivaling Franklin Roosevelt's in 1932. What is the strongest basis for the comparison?
options: (A) Both repudiated the old philosophy and installed a new answer to what government is for.
(B) Both winning candidates came from the same hometown.
(C) Both elections were decided by the Supreme Court.
(D) Neither of the two elections had any real lasting significance for American governance at all.
explanation: 1932 and 1980 are mirror images: Roosevelt repudiated laissez-faire and built the activist state; Reagan repudiated the activist state and began dismantling it. Both elections didn't just change parties — they changed the philosophy of government for a generation, which is what makes 'revolution' the right word for each.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It states the structural parallel the comparison rests on: philosophical repudiation plus a new governing answer, in opposite directions.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Roosevelt was from New York, Reagan from Illinois and California; biography is not the basis of the comparison.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Neither election was decided by the Supreme Court; both were clear electoral victories.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Both elections reshaped American governance for decades; insignificance is the opposite of the historical judgment.

stem: The chart shows federal deficits giving way to surpluses by 1998. What ended the Reagan-era pattern of large peacetime deficits?

chart_spec.title: Federal Budget Deficit (+) / Surplus (−), 1980–2000

options: (A) The abolition of all federal taxes in 1995.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Taxes were raised, not abolished; the 1990 and 1993 deals increased revenue.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The military remained enormous; deficit reduction came from taxes, restraint, and growth, not disarmament.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It names the actual policy combination behind the chart's turnaround: bipartisan budget deals plus boom-time revenues.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The chart plainly shows negative values — surpluses — in 1998 and 2000.
